title: Chronic Inflammatory Skin Conditions
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Chronic inflammatory skin disease is where immunology becomes visible. This chapter works through rosacea, lichen planus, and psoriasis, then adds pyoderma gangrenosum, hidradenitis suppurativa, and the alopecias, because the exam groups them by mechanism rather than by appearance. For each one, follow the chain from the immune cell and cytokine to the histologic change to the physical finding, since the question usually gives you a lesion and a location and asks for the mechanism, the biopsy, or the systemic disease it accompanies. The distinctions that earn points are mechanistic: innate neurovascular inflammation versus a cytotoxic T cell interface attack versus a Th17 proliferative loop versus pure neutrophil activation.
prerequisites: Layers of the epidermis, keratinocyte maturation, and the dermal-epidermal junction (IN-1)
Structure of the hair follicle, sebaceous gland, and apocrine gland, and the hair cycle (IN-2)
Innate immunity: antimicrobial peptides, neutrophil chemotaxis, IL-1, IL-8, and TNF
Helper T cell subsets and their cytokines, especially Th17, plus CD8 cytotoxic killing by perforin, granzyme, and Fas
Basic patterns of inflammation and repair: acanthosis, apoptosis, granulation tissue, and fibrosis

connections.how: Psoriasis is the clearest human example of an IL-23 and Th17 axis disease, and lichen planus is a model of CD8 mediated interface injury, so the same cytokine maps are tested in both subjects.
Pyoderma gangrenosum and erythema nodosum are extraintestinal manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease, and lichen planus is associated with hepatitis C infection.
Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy with distal interphalangeal and enthesis involvement, and pyoderma gangrenosum travels with rheumatoid arthritis.
Androgenetic alopecia and hidradenitis suppurativa both depend on postpubertal androgen signaling, including conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha reductase.
Pyoderma gangrenosum can accompany myelodysplastic syndrome and other myeloid disorders, so a neutrophilic dermatosis can be the presenting sign of marrow disease.

terms.def: A pattern in which lymphocytes mass along the dermal-epidermal junction and injure the basal keratinocyte layer.
Thickening of the viable epidermis, usually from keratinocyte hyperproliferation.
Retention of keratinocyte nuclei in the stratum corneum, indicating that cells reached the surface before completing maturation.
Thickening of the stratum granulosum, the opposite of the granular layer loss seen in psoriasis.
An apoptotic basal keratinocyte seen as a rounded eosinophilic (colloid) body at or below the junction.
A collection of neutrophils within the parakeratotic stratum corneum, characteristic of psoriasis.
The thin shelf of epidermis lying over a dermal papilla, thinned in psoriasis so that papillary capillaries bleed easily.
Appearance of new lesions of an existing skin disease at a site of trauma, seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo.
Worsening or new ulceration of a neutrophilic dermatosis after minor trauma, needle puncture, or debridement.
A plugged follicular orifice, open (blackhead) or closed (whitehead), present in acne vulgaris and absent in rosacea.
The actively growing phase of the hair cycle, followed by catagen involution and telogen rest.
The normally low antigen presentation and reduced MHC class I expression of the anagen hair bulb, lost in alopecia areata.

sections.title: Rosacea: neurovascular and innate immune inflammation of central facial skin

blocks.text: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disorder confined almost entirely to the convexities of the central face: cheeks, nose, chin, glabella, and forehead. It typically begins in adults between about 30 and 50 years of age and is most common in fair-skinned people. The distribution is a clue to the mechanism, because central facial skin carries a dense superficial vascular plexus, abundant sebaceous glands, and a rich supply of sensory nerve endings.

Two processes run together. The first is neurovascular dysregulation. Sensory nerve endings in facial skin express transient receptor potential channels, including TRPV1, which respond to heat, capsaicin, ethanol, and inflammatory mediators. When these channels open, the nerve releases vasoactive neuropeptides such as substance P and calcitonin gene related peptide, which dilate the superficial plexus and increase permeability. Early on this produces transient flushing. With repeated episodes the vessels remain dilated and elongated, so the erythema becomes fixed and visible telangiectasias appear.

The second process is innate immune overactivation. Rosacea skin contains increased cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide and increased activity of the serine protease kallikrein 5, which cleaves cathelicidin into fragments such as LL-37. These fragments are chemotactic for neutrophils, stimulate keratinocyte cytokine release, and promote angiogenesis, which is why papules and sterile pustules can sit on a background of erythema. Toll-like receptor 2 signaling, ultraviolet damage, and increased density of the follicular mite Demodex folliculorum are all thought to feed this loop, although Demodex is a correlation rather than an established cause.

blocks.title: Trigger to fixed erythema in rosacea
steps: Trigger: heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, stress
TRPV1 and related channels open on facial sensory nerves
Substance P and CGRP released; superficial plexus dilates
Flushing with plasma leakage and mediator delivery
Cathelicidin and kallikrein 5 activity rise; LL-37 recruits neutrophils
Vessels remodel and stay dilated: fixed erythema and telangiectasias
Remodeled, inflamed skin responds to the next trigger more easily
blocks.caption: Repeated flushing becomes persistent erythema because vascular remodeling and innate inflammation reinforce each other.

blocks.text: Because the inflammation is centered on vessels and the perifollicular dermis rather than on a plugged follicular orifice, comedones never form. Their absence is the single most useful negative finding in rosacea. Biopsy, which is rarely needed, shows dilated dermal vessels, lymphohistiocytic perivascular and perifollicular inflammation, dermal edema, and solar elastosis, with neutrophils in and around follicles when pustules are present.

blocks.title: Rosacea phenotypes and the mechanism behind each
rows: Flushing, persistent central erythema, telangiectasias, stinging
Inflammatory papules and sterile pustules on erythema, no comedones
Cathelicidin and LL-37 driven neutrophil recruitment
Rhinophyma: bulbous, thickened nose with patulous follicles
Years of inflammation drive sebaceous hyperplasia and dermal fibrosis
Blepharitis, conjunctival injection, gritty or foreign body sensation, chalazia
Meibomian gland inflammation and obstruction with tear film instability
blocks.caption: Phenotypes overlap in the same patient; rhinophyma and ocular disease are the complications to predict.

blocks.text: Two complications are heavily tested. Rhinophyma is sebaceous and fibrous overgrowth of the nose, produced by sustained inflammation and lymphatic obstruction, and it occurs mostly in men. Ocular rosacea affects a large minority of patients and can precede the skin findings, so eye symptoms in an adult with facial flushing belong to the same diagnosis rather than to a separate problem.

sections.title: Separating rosacea from acne vulgaris, seborrheic dermatitis, and the malar rash of lupus

blocks.text: Four conditions produce central facial redness, and each has one mechanistic feature that settles the question. Acne vulgaris begins with follicular hyperkeratinization and sebum retention, so the primary lesion is a comedo. Rosacea begins in vessels and nerves, so there is no comedo. Seborrheic dermatitis is an inflammatory response to Malassezia yeast in sebum-rich skin, so it produces greasy scale and it concentrates in the folds and creases. Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is immune complex and interface injury triggered by ultraviolet light, so it spares the shaded nasolabial folds and comes with systemic findings.

blocks.title: Central facial eruptions compared
rows: Young to middle-aged adults, mostly women
Open and closed comedones, then papules, pustules, nodules
Erythematous patches with greasy yellow scale
Confluent erythematous to edematous malar patch
Follicular plugging, Cutibacterium acnes, androgen-driven sebum
None usually; consider hyperandrogenism if severe
Severe or refractory disease with HIV or Parkinson disease
Arthralgia, cytopenias, nephritis, positive ANA and anti-dsDNA
blocks.caption: Comedones, scale, and the nasolabial folds separate these four faster than overall redness does.

blocks.text: The nasolabial fold rule is worth understanding rather than memorizing. The fold is a crease that shades itself from direct sunlight, so a photosensitive eruption such as acute cutaneous lupus tends to stop at it. Seborrheic dermatitis follows sebaceous gland density and the retention of yeast and sebum within creases, so the same fold is a favored site. Rosacea follows the convex, vessel-rich central face and so sits between the two patterns.

Two further distinctions appear on examinations. Perioral dermatitis presents as small papules and pustules around the mouth with a clear rim of skin at the vermilion border, often after topical corticosteroid use, and it lacks both telangiectasias and comedones. Steroid-induced rosacea-like eruptions worsen after each withdrawal of a topical corticosteroid, which is a mechanistic clue rather than a separate disease: corticosteroids suppress inflammation while thinning the dermis and promoting vasodilation, so the underlying erythema rebounds. A useful ordering question is therefore which structure the eruption begins in: the follicular orifice in acne, the sebaceous crease in seborrheic dermatitis, the superficial vascular plexus and sensory nerves in rosacea, and the basal layer of sun-exposed skin in acute cutaneous lupus.

blocks.predict: An adult reports that wine and hot soup turn the cheeks and nose red within minutes, and you see fine dilated vessels but no blackheads or whiteheads. Which one finding rules out acne vulgaris, and which rules out the lupus malar rash?

sections.title: Lichen planus: cytotoxic interface attack on basal keratinocytes

blocks.text: Lichen planus is the prototype of interface dermatitis caused by CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes. The cells recognize an antigen presented on basal keratinocytes, accumulate in a dense band immediately beneath and within the basal layer, and kill those keratinocytes by apoptosis using perforin, granzyme, Fas ligand, and TNF. Every classic finding of the disease follows from that single event.

The clinical lesion is summarized by six words beginning with the letter P: pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques. They favor the flexor wrists and forearms, the shins, the ankles, and the genitals, and they can appear along a scratch or scar, which is the Koebner phenomenon. Fine white reticulated lines called Wickham striae cross the surface. In the mouth, lichen planus produces a white lacy network on the buccal mucosa, and erosive oral and genital forms are painful rather than itchy. Nail involvement can produce longitudinal ridging, thinning, and in severe cases a dorsal pterygium from scarring of the matrix.

blocks.title: From T cell attack to the visible papule
steps: CD8 T cells recognize antigen on basal keratinocytes
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate forms at the dermal-epidermal junction
Basal keratinocytes undergo apoptosis and become Civatte bodies
Basal layer damage produces a sawtooth contour of the rete ridges
Melanin released from dying cells is taken up by dermal macrophages
Surviving epidermis thickens its granular layer (hypergranulosis)
Result: flat violaceous polygonal papules with Wickham striae
blocks.caption: One cytotoxic event at the junction explains the color, the shape, the surface lines, and the biopsy.

blocks.text: Biopsy findings map one to one onto the mechanism. The band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugs the junction. Apoptotic basal keratinocytes appear as rounded eosinophilic Civatte bodies, also called colloid bodies. Loss of the normal basal layer leaves the rete ridges with a pointed, sawtooth outline. Hypergranulosis thickens the stratum granulosum, and because the granular layer is where keratohyalin granules concentrate, this thickening is what shows through as the white Wickham striae. The violaceous color has two sources: the dense cellular infiltrate itself, and pigment incontinence, meaning melanin dropped from dying basal cells into the papillary dermis. Compact orthokeratosis, not parakeratosis, covers the surface, which is the opposite of psoriasis.

Lichen planus is associated with chronic hepatitis C virus infection, particularly the oral form and particularly in certain populations, and the association is strong enough that board questions pair lacy buccal lesions with abnormal liver enzymes. Lichenoid drug eruptions look similar but tend to be more photodistributed and to contain eosinophils in the infiltrate, and graft versus host disease produces the same interface pattern through the same cytotoxic mechanism in an allogeneic setting. Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation that lasts months after the papules flatten is expected, again because of pigment incontinence.

sections.title: Psoriasis: the IL-23 and Th17 loop and its clinical signature

blocks.text: Psoriasis is an immune-driven disorder of keratinocyte proliferation. Genetic susceptibility is strong, with concordance in monozygotic twins of roughly two thirds and with HLA-Cw6 (HLA-C*06:02) as the classic associated allele, strongest in early-onset plaque disease. A trigger such as mechanical trauma, streptococcal pharyngitis, certain drugs including lithium and beta blockers, or withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids activates dermal dendritic cells in susceptible skin.

Activated dendritic cells release IL-23 and TNF. IL-23 expands and sustains Th17 lymphocytes, which secrete IL-17A and IL-22. IL-17 acts directly on keratinocytes, driving them to proliferate and to release chemokines such as CXCL8 (IL-8) along with antimicrobial peptides. Those chemokines recruit neutrophils and more T cells into the lesion, and the recruited cells supply more cytokine, so the loop sustains itself. TNF amplifies each step. Epidermal transit time, normally about four weeks from basal layer to shed corneocyte, falls to a few days.

blocks.title: The self-sustaining psoriatic loop
steps: Genetic risk plus trigger activates dermal dendritic cells
Dendritic cells secrete IL-23 and TNF
IL-23 expands Th17 cells
Th17 cells release IL-17A and IL-22
Keratinocytes proliferate and release chemokines and antimicrobial peptides
Neutrophils and T cells are recruited into epidermis and dermis
Recruited cells deliver more IL-23 and TNF, restarting the loop
blocks.caption: Because the output of the loop recruits cells that feed its input, psoriatic plaques persist without any ongoing external trigger.

blocks.text: Clinically this produces sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery-white scale. Plaques favor extensor surfaces, especially elbows and knees, along with the scalp, the lumbosacral area and gluteal cleft, and the umbilicus. The sharp border reflects the abrupt edge of the proliferating population, and the silvery scale is thick stratum corneum made of immature corneocytes. New plaques appearing in a scratch, a surgical scar, or a sunburn line is the Koebner phenomenon, explained by trauma-released antimicrobial peptides and cytokines activating the same loop in previously normal skin.

blocks.title: Psoriasis variants and features to recognize
rows: Extensor plaques with silvery scale, most common form
Established IL-23 and Th17 loop in chronic lesions
Abrupt small drop-like papules in children or young adults
Follows streptococcal pharyngitis, with molecular mimicry between M protein and keratin
Shiny erythema in axillae, groin, and inframammary folds with little scale
Moisture and occlusion in folds prevent the usual dry scale
Sterile pustules or near-total body erythema with systemic illness
Massive neutrophil recruitment, with fluid, protein, and heat loss across a failed barrier
Pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discoloration, subungual hyperkeratosis
Inflammation in the nail matrix (pitting) or the nail bed (oil drop, onycholysis)
Distal interphalangeal arthritis, dactylitis, enthesitis, pencil-in-cup erosions
Seronegative spondyloarthropathy sharing the IL-23 and IL-17 axis; nail disease raises the risk
blocks.caption: Nail findings matter because they predict joint disease: pitting comes from matrix inflammation, oil-drop change from nail bed inflammation.

blocks.text: Psoriasis also behaves as a systemic inflammatory disease. Moderate to severe disease is independently associated with metabolic syndrome and with cardiovascular events, which is attributed to the circulating burden of TNF and IL-17 driven inflammation and its effect on insulin signaling and the endothelium.

sections.title: Psoriasis histology and the mechanical basis of the Auspitz sign

blocks.text: Every histologic feature of a psoriatic plaque is a consequence of accelerated keratinocyte turnover plus neutrophil recruitment, so the slide can be reconstructed from the mechanism rather than memorized as a list.

blocks.title: Psoriasis histology: finding, cause, and clinical correlate
rows: Acanthosis with regular, uniform elongation of the rete ridges
Sustained IL-17 driven proliferation of the basal compartment
Parakeratosis (retained nuclei in the stratum corneum)
Transit time falls from about four weeks to a few days, so cells reach the surface immature
Loose, friable, silvery scale rather than normal invisible shedding
Cells pass through the granular stage too quickly to accumulate keratohyalin granules
Scale that detaches in sheets instead of being tightly bound
Rete ridges elongate downward while the epidermis over each papilla stays thin
Mechanical basis of the Auspitz sign
Angiogenesis driven by VEGF released from activated keratinocytes
Bright erythema of the plaque and the bleeding source for the Auspitz sign
Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in the stratum corneum)
Keratinocyte chemokines such as CXCL8 draw neutrophils all the way through the epidermis
Spongiform pustule of Kogoj (neutrophils in the spinous layer)
The same chemotaxis caught at an earlier level of the epidermis
Supports the diagnosis, especially in pustular psoriasis
blocks.caption: Two processes, fast turnover and neutrophil chemotaxis, generate the entire histologic picture.

blocks.text: The Auspitz sign deserves a careful mechanical explanation because it is a favorite question. In normal skin the epidermis over each dermal papilla is a reasonably thick shelf, and the capillary loop inside the papilla is protected. In psoriasis the rete ridges elongate downward between the papillae while the epidermis directly above each papilla is stretched and thinned, so the papillae rise into a shallow space covered only by a thin suprapapillary plate. The capillary loops inside those papillae are simultaneously dilated and more fragile. Removing the adherent scale shears away that thin plate, the exposed capillary loops rupture, and pinpoint droplets of blood appear across the surface.

blocks.title: Reading one biopsy two ways
blocks.text: A specimen shows a thickened epidermis, no granular layer, nuclei retained in the stratum corneum, and neutrophils sitting in that corneum. A second specimen shows a thickened granular layer, compact keratin without retained nuclei, a dense band of lymphocytes at the junction, and scattered apoptotic basal cells. The first is psoriasis: proliferation outruns maturation, so maturation markers (granular layer, enucleated corneocytes) are lost, and chemokines pull neutrophils to the surface. The second is lichen planus: proliferation is normal but the basal layer is under cytotoxic attack, so maturation is intact or exaggerated and the infiltrate is lymphocytic at the junction. Granular layer status alone separates them: lost in psoriasis, thickened in lichen planus.

One caution applies to grattage, the gentle scraping used to elicit these signs. Scale that comes away in fine silvery flakes before bleeding appears is sometimes called the candle wax sign, and the pinpoint bleeding that follows is the Auspitz sign. Trauma to psoriatic skin can itself seed new plaques through the Koebner phenomenon, so the same maneuver that demonstrates the sign demonstrates the mechanism.

sections.title: Pyoderma gangrenosum: a sterile neutrophilic dermatosis

blocks.text: Pyoderma gangrenosum is named misleadingly. It is neither pyogenic in the infectious sense nor gangrenous: it is a neutrophilic dermatosis, meaning a sterile inflammatory disease in which activated neutrophils accumulate in tissue and destroy it. Cultures from an untreated lesion are negative and no organism is found on special stains.

The driving abnormality is dysregulated innate immunity. Overproduction of IL-1 beta, together with IL-8 (CXCL8), IL-17, and TNF, recruits neutrophils and prolongs their survival, and neutrophil function itself appears abnormal in many patients. Released proteases, reactive oxygen species, and matrix metalloproteinases digest dermal collagen, so the lesion becomes a deep ulcer rather than a superficial erosion. Several monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes that cause pyoderma gangrenosum are driven by inflammasome dysregulation, which supports the IL-1 mechanism.

blocks.title: Natural history of a pyoderma gangrenosum lesion
steps: Small tender pustule, nodule, or papule appears, often on the lower leg
Lesion breaks down centrally
Neutrophil proteases digest dermal collagen and the ulcer deepens
Border becomes violaceous and undermined, with epidermis overhanging the base
Ulcer expands centrifugally with a boggy, purulent-appearing base that is sterile
Healing leaves a characteristic thin cribriform (sieve-like) scar
blocks.caption: The undermined violaceous border and the cribriform scar are the two most recognizable features.

blocks.text: Pathergy is the behavior that identifies the disease. Minor trauma, a needle puncture, a biopsy site, or surgical debridement delivers fresh chemotactic signals into already primed tissue, so the lesion enlarges instead of healing. The clinical consequence is diagnostically useful: an ulcer that grows after debridement is behaving like a neutrophilic dermatosis, not like an infected wound. Biopsy shows a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with abscess formation, necrosis, and often a secondary leukocytoclastic vasculitis, with no organisms on special stains and no growth on culture. Because the histology is suggestive rather than specific, diagnosis requires excluding infection, venous and arterial ulceration, vasculitis, and malignancy.

blocks.title: Systemic associations and why they travel together
rows: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis
Shared neutrophil-driven mucocutaneous inflammation; one of several extraintestinal manifestations
Chronic TNF and IL-1 driven inflammation with neutrophil recruitment into tissue
Myelodysplastic syndrome, acute and chronic myeloid leukemia, monoclonal gammopathy (IgA)
Abnormal myeloid clones produce functionally abnormal neutrophils and excess myeloid cytokines
Inflammasome dysregulation with excess IL-1 beta signaling
blocks.caption: In roughly half of cases a systemic disease is present, so the ulcer can be the presenting sign of bowel or marrow disease.

blocks.text: Distinguish pyoderma gangrenosum from two mimics. Sweet syndrome is also a neutrophilic dermatosis and shares the malignancy associations, but it produces tender edematous plaques with fever rather than deep ulcers. Necrotizing infection produces rapidly spreading pain, systemic toxicity, and positive cultures, and organisms are demonstrable on Gram stain and tissue culture.

sections.title: Hidradenitis suppurativa: follicular occlusion in apocrine-bearing skin

blocks.text: Hidradenitis suppurativa was once attributed to primary apocrine gland infection, and the name still reflects that idea. Current understanding places the initiating lesion in the hair follicle. Hyperkeratosis and infundibular plugging obstruct the terminal follicle in intertriginous skin, the occluded follicle dilates under retained keratin and sebum, and it eventually ruptures into the dermis. Apocrine glands are involved secondarily because they drain into the same follicular unit, which explains the distribution without making the gland the cause.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of hidradenitis suppurativa
steps: Follicular hyperkeratosis plugs terminal follicles in axilla, groin, perineum, inframammary skin
Occluded follicle dilates as keratin and sebum accumulate
Follicular wall ruptures, spilling keratin, sebum, and commensal bacteria into dermis
Keratin and bacterial products trigger IL-1, TNF, and IL-17 driven neutrophilic inflammation
Painful deep nodules and sterile or secondarily infected abscesses form
Repeated rupture and re-epithelialization create epithelium-lined sinus tracts
Chronic healing produces rope-like fibrotic bands and contracture
blocks.caption: Occlusion, rupture, inflammation, and tract formation, in that order, explain every physical finding.

blocks.text: Onset is after puberty, usually in the second or third decade, and women are affected more often than men. The disease is restricted to flexural, apocrine-bearing skin: axillae, inguinal folds, perineum and perianal skin, buttocks, and inframammary skin. Lesions are deep, painful, and recurrent, and they differ from a simple furuncle in three ways: they recur in the same sites, they interconnect through sinus tracts that drain foul-smelling material, and they heal with hypertrophic and rope-like scars. Double-ended (tombstone) comedones with two or more orifices sharing a dilated follicular space are a hallmark of chronic disease.

blocks.title: Risk factors and the mechanism each contributes
rows: Increases skin-on-skin friction, moisture, and occlusion in folds, and adds adipose-derived inflammatory cytokines
Nicotine promotes follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging, and alters neutrophil and keratinocyte signaling
Androgen-dependent follicular and glandular activity explains onset after puberty
A minority of cases carry gamma-secretase (nicastrin, PSEN1, PSENEN) variants affecting follicular differentiation
Repeated trauma to the follicular infundibulum promotes occlusion and rupture
blocks.caption: Obesity and smoking are the two risk factors most often tested, and both act through follicular occlusion.

blocks.text: Long-standing disease carries real structural consequences: lymphedema of the affected region from scarring of lymphatics, anal and urethral fistulas in perineal disease, restricted limb movement from contracture, secondary amyloidosis from chronic inflammation, and squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronically inflamed and scarred perineal or buttock skin. The follicular occlusion tetrad (hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata, dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, and pilonidal sinus) groups the diseases that share this mechanism in different sites.

sections.title: Alopecias: which part of the hair cycle fails, and whether the follicle survives

blocks.text: Hair grows in cycles. Anagen is the growth phase and lasts about two to six years on the scalp, catagen is a brief involution phase, and telogen is a resting phase of about three months that ends when the club hair is shed. At any moment roughly 85 to 90 percent of scalp follicles are in anagen, and shedding of up to about 100 hairs daily is normal. Place any alopecia by asking which phase is disturbed and whether the bulge stem cells survive.

The second question separates the two major categories. Nonscarring alopecia leaves follicular ostia visible on the scalp surface, so regrowth remains possible. Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia destroys the bulge stem cells and replaces the follicle with fibrous tissue, so the scalp becomes smooth and shiny with no visible openings and the loss is permanent. Looking for follicular openings is therefore the single most informative step in examining hair loss.

blocks.title: Alopecias by mechanism
rows: Autoreactive CD8 T cell attack on the anagen bulb after loss of follicular immune privilege
Round or oval smooth patches, exclamation point hairs tapering toward the scalp, nail pitting
Dihydrotestosterone shortens anagen and miniaturizes androgen-sensitive follicles
Vertex and frontotemporal recession in men, widened central part with retained frontal line in women
A stressor synchronously shifts many anagen follicles into telogen
Diffuse shedding of club hairs about two to four months after the event, positive gentle pull test
Abrupt arrest of mitosis in the matrix, as with cytotoxic chemotherapy
Rapid diffuse loss within days to weeks, broken tapered shafts
Marginal thinning, early nonscarring and late scarring
Lichen planopilaris and discoid lupus erythematosus
Lymphocytic attack on the follicular bulge and infundibulum
Perifollicular erythema and scale, then smooth patches without ostia
blocks.caption: Place any case by naming the disturbed phase or target, then checking whether follicular ostia remain.

blocks.text: Three mechanisms deserve explanation. In alopecia areata the anagen bulb normally enjoys immune privilege through low MHC class I expression and local immunosuppressive signals; when that privilege is lost, autoreactive CD8 T cells attack the bulb. The shaft narrows where growth was disrupted and breaks near the surface as the exclamation point hair, but the bulge stem cells survive, so regrowth can occur. In androgenetic alopecia, 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which in genetically sensitive scalp follicles shortens successive anagen phases, so each cycle yields a shorter, finer, less pigmented shaft until a terminal hair becomes a vellus hair; occipital follicles lack this sensitivity, which is why the occipital fringe persists. In telogen effluvium an insult such as childbirth, major surgery, high fever, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, or rapid weight loss pushes many follicles into telogen at once, and because telogen lasts about three months the shedding appears only two to four months later.

blocks.title: Three patterns of diffuse or patchy loss
blocks.text: A woman sheds large amounts of hair four months after a complicated delivery, with normal scalp skin and visible ostia: telogen effluvium, from synchronized entry into telogen, expected to recover. A young man has two sharply round smooth patches with short tapered hairs at the margins and fine nail pitting: alopecia areata, from an immune attack on anagen bulbs, with ostia preserved. A middle-aged woman has smooth shiny patches at the vertex with perifollicular scale, no visible ostia, and violaceous papules on her wrists: lichen planopilaris, the scarring scalp counterpart of lichen planus, with permanent loss because the bulge stem cells are destroyed.

Tinea capitis and trichotillomania both produce patchy loss with broken hairs, but tinea adds scale, inflammation, and sometimes a boggy kerion, while trichotillomania shows hairs broken at varying lengths in an irregular pattern. Alopecia areata also associates with autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, and type 1 diabetes, which fits its autoimmune mechanism.

integration.text: These diseases are best organized by immune mechanism rather than by appearance, because the mechanism predicts the histology, the associated systemic disease, and the behavior of the lesion. Innate neurovascular inflammation with cathelicidin activation gives rosacea its flushing, fixed erythema, and comedo-free pustules. A CD8 cytotoxic attack at the dermal-epidermal junction gives lichen planus its Civatte bodies, sawtooth rete ridges, and violaceous color from pigment incontinence. An IL-23 and Th17 loop gives psoriasis fast keratinocyte turnover, so maturation markers are lost (absent granular layer, parakeratosis) while chemokines pull neutrophils into the corneum. Pure neutrophil activation without a microbe gives pyoderma gangrenosum its sterile, protease-driven, pathergic ulcer. Follicular occlusion with rupture gives hidradenitis suppurativa its tracts and scars. Loss of follicular immune privilege, androgen sensitivity, cycle synchronization, and stem cell destruction account for the alopecias.

Skin findings also function as a window on other organ systems, which is why these conditions appear in integration questions. Lacy oral lichen planus raises the question of hepatitis C. A pathergic leg ulcer points at ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, or a myeloid neoplasm. Nail pitting in psoriasis predicts a seronegative arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints, and severe psoriasis tracks with metabolic and cardiovascular risk. Scarring alopecia on the scalp with violaceous papules on the wrists is one disease in two locations. The limits are worth stating plainly: these associations are statistical rather than universal, histology in rosacea, pyoderma gangrenosum, and hidradenitis suppurativa is supportive rather than diagnostic, and pyoderma gangrenosum in particular remains a diagnosis of exclusion that requires ruling out infection, vascular ulceration, vasculitis, and malignancy.

summary: Rosacea is adult central facial flushing, fixed erythema, telangiectasias, and pustules without comedones, from TRPV1 driven neurovascular reactivity plus kallikrein 5 and cathelicidin activation; predict rhinophyma and ocular rosacea.
Comedones mean acne vulgaris, greasy scale in the nasolabial folds means seborrheic dermatitis, and sparing of the nasolabial folds with systemic findings means the acute lupus malar rash.
Lichen planus is a CD8 interface dermatitis: pruritic purple polygonal planar papules with Wickham striae and lacy buccal lesions, and an association with hepatitis C.
Lichen planus histology follows from basal keratinocyte apoptosis: band-like junctional lymphocytes, Civatte bodies, sawtooth rete ridges, hypergranulosis, and pigment incontinence.

Psoriasis is a self-sustaining loop in which dendritic cell IL-23 expands Th17 cells whose IL-17 and IL-22, with TNF, drive keratinocyte proliferation and neutrophil recruitment; HLA-Cw6 is the classic allele.

Psoriasis plaques are sharply demarcated with silvery scale on extensors, scalp, and lumbosacral skin, with Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting that predicts psoriatic arthritis, and guttate disease after streptococcal pharyngitis.

Psoriasis histology is fast turnover plus chemotaxis: acanthosis with regularly elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, lost granular layer, and Munro microabscesses; thin suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries explain the Auspitz sign.
Granular layer status separates the two papulosquamous patterns: lost in psoriasis, thickened in lichen planus.

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a sterile neutrophilic dermatosis forming a painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that worsens after trauma (pathergy), linked to inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and myeloid neoplasms.

Hidradenitis suppurativa is follicular occlusion and rupture in axillary, inguinal, and perineal skin producing nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and rope-like scars, with obesity and smoking as the main risk factors; alopecias are classified by the hair cycle phase affected and by whether follicular ostia survive.

verify: Nomenclature for rosacea has shifted from four numbered subtypes to a phenotype-based scheme; confirm which terminology NABNE expects.
The causal role of Demodex folliculorum in rosacea is still debated and is presented here as an association, not an established cause.
Reported frequency of ocular involvement in rosacea ranges widely across sources (often quoted from about 30 to 60 percent), so no single figure is stated.
The strength of the lichen planus and hepatitis C association varies substantially by population and is strongest for oral lichen planus; confirm the emphasis NABNE places on it.
HLA-Cw6 is written as HLA-C*06:02 in current nomenclature; confirm which form appears on the examination.
Monozygotic twin concordance in psoriasis is quoted from roughly 35 to 70 percent in different series; the text says about two thirds as an upper consensus estimate.
The proportion of pyoderma gangrenosum cases with an associated systemic disease is quoted from about 50 to 70 percent across sources.

Hair cycle values (anagen duration, telogen about three months, roughly 85 to 90 percent of follicles in anagen, up to about 100 hairs shed daily) are consensus approximations that differ slightly between texts.
Normal epidermal transit time is quoted from about 26 to 28 days up to about 40 days depending on the source; psoriatic transit time of a few days is consistent across sources.
